items.followUp: Compare NADH and FADH₂ in their ATP yield during cellular respiration.

rubric.why: Gives the textbook ATP yield for NADH.
rubric.description: NADH produces 3 ATP in the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct NADH yield.

rubric.why: Gives the textbook ATP yield for FADH₂.
rubric.description: FADH₂ produces 2 ATP in the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct FADH₂ yield.

modelAnswer: NADH and FADH₂ are reduced coenzymes that carry hydrogen/electrons to the electron transport chain.
In the textbook’s ATP accounting, one NADH produces 3 ATP, while one FADH₂ produces 2 ATP.

items.followUp: Define glycolysis and state its end product.

rubric.why: Identifies the substrate and the breakdown product of glycolysis.
rubric.description: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose into pyruvic acid (pyruvate).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying glucose breakdown to pyruvic acid/pyruvate.

rubric.why: Provides the site of glycolysis, a key part of its definition.
rubric.description: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct site.

modelAnswer: Glycolysis is the breakdown of one glucose molecule into two molecules of pyruvic acid in the cytoplasm.
Its end product is two molecules of pyruvic acid (pyruvate).

items.followUp: Explain how temperature affects enzyme activity.

rubric.why: States that enzymes work best at a particular pH.
rubric.description: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which its activity is greatest.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the optimum-pH effect.

rubric.why: Explains how a pH change lowers enzyme activity.
rubric.description: A pH away from the optimum alters the enzyme’s structure or active site; extreme pH can denature it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the structural change or loss of activity.

modelAnswer: Each enzyme works fastest at its particular optimum pH.
A pH above or below the optimum changes the enzyme’s structure and active site, so its activity decreases; extreme pH may denature it.

items.followUp: What is enzyme denaturation, and what happens to the enzyme’s active site?

rubric.why: Defines denaturation as a change in enzyme structure.
rubric.description: Denaturation is a change in an enzyme’s structure, usually caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the structural change and/or its cause.

rubric.why: States the effect of denaturation on enzyme function.
rubric.description: The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme loses activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the loss of substrate binding or activity.

modelAnswer: Denaturation is a change in an enzyme’s structure, usually caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
The active site changes shape, so the substrate cannot bind properly and the enzyme loses its activity.

items.followUp: State the direction in which arteries and veins carry blood.

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of blood flow in arteries.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of blood flow in veins.
rubric.description: Veins carry blood towards the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction.

modelAnswer: Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
Veins are blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart.

items.followUp: Where is pericardial fluid found, and how does it protect the heart?

rubric.why: States the fluid’s lubricating function.
rubric.description: Pericardial fluid reduces friction as the heart beats.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for reducing friction or lubrication.

rubric.why: Connects the fluid’s function to the beating heart.
rubric.description: It allows the heart to move smoothly within the pericardium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining smooth movement during beating.

modelAnswer: Pericardial fluid lies between the membranes surrounding the heart.
It lubricates the surfaces, reduces friction and allows the heart to beat smoothly.

items.followUp: Describe unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Describes an organism made of one cell that carries out life processes.
rubric.description: A unicellular organism consists of one cell that performs all life functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature of unicellular organisms.

rubric.why: Identifies organisms whose cells live together in a colony.
rubric.description: Colonial organisms consist of similar cells living together; Volvox is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the colonial organization and/or an appropriate example.

rubric.why: Identifies the many-cell organization and cell specialization.
rubric.description: Multicellular organisms have many cells, often specialized for different functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature of multicellular organisms.

rubric.why: Explains how specialization organizes work in multicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Specialized cells work together, showing division of labour and forming tissues and organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for division of labour or the organization into tissues and organs.

modelAnswer: In unicellular organisms, a single cell performs all the functions needed for life; for example, Amoeba.
In colonial organisms, similar cells live together in a group or colony; Volvox is an example.
Multicellular organisms consist of many cells, often specialized for different functions; humans are an example.
Specialized cells work together through division of labour and may form tissues and organs.

items.followUp: Explain how humidity, wind and the number of stomata affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Describes the effects of environmental conditions that promote transpiration.
rubric.description: Bright light and higher temperature generally increase transpiration.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for explaining two relevant environmental factors and their effects.

rubric.why: Explains the effects of humidity and air movement on water-vapour loss.
rubric.description: Low humidity and wind generally increase transpiration; high humidity lowers it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining humidity or wind.

rubric.why: Connects the plant’s water supply to transpiration.
rubric.description: Adequate soil water supports transpiration, while water shortage causes stomata to close or the plant to wilt.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the effect of water availability.

rubric.why: Describes structural features of the leaf that influence transpiration.
rubric.description: A larger leaf area or more stomata increases transpiration, whereas a thick cuticle reduces it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct leaf-structure factor and its effect.

modelAnswer: Light: bright light usually opens stomata and increases transpiration; darkness generally lowers it.
Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and usually raises the rate of transpiration.
Humidity: low humidity increases transpiration, while high humidity reduces the difference in water-vapour concentration and lowers it.
Wind: moving air removes moist air around the leaf, usually increasing transpiration.
Soil water: adequate water supply supports transpiration; water shortage may cause stomata to close and reduce it.
Leaf features: larger leaf area and more stomata generally increase transpiration, while a thick waxy cuticle reduces water loss.
